paragraphs: This paper studies how a robot can learn the meanings of sentences through its own behavior. The focus is compositionality: understanding a sentence by combining the meanings of its words. The proposed connectionist model links this linguistic ability to embodiment, so that learned meanings fit the robot’s particular sensory and motor capabilities.

The central proposal is that these meanings can organize themselves through general relationships between sentences and behavioral patterns. Sentence meanings are therefore connected to what the robot experiences and does. Learning correspondences across examples is intended to provide a basis for interpreting combinations of words that the robot has not previously encountered.

Simple experiments with a real robot support this claim. The robot produces corresponding behaviors for unlearned sentences by drawing analogies with previously learned sentence–behavior relationships. This demonstrates the proposed form of generalization within the simple language and experiments studied. Its significance is that compositional understanding and bodily experience can develop together within one learned representation.
neurips-2003-a-holistic-approach-to-comp.tldr: A connectionist model learns embodied sentence meanings that let a real robot respond to previously unlearned sentences in simple experiments.

paragraphs: Objects at different depths appear at slightly different positions in the two eyes. This binocular disparity provides the signal studied here. The paper implements a model of a visual cortical complex cell that responds selectively to disparity, translating the binocular energy model into a system built from silicon circuits and spiking neurons.

Two chips contain neurons with Gabor-type spatial receptive fields, which describe how each neuron responds to patterns seen by one eye. Additional circuits combine their spike outputs to produce a disparity-selective response. The preferred disparity can be changed by shifting either the positions or the phases of the two eyes’ receptive-field profiles, matching two mechanisms used in biology.

The implemented system performs better when disparity is encoded through phase shifts. The stated reason is that responses across neurons tuned to different disparities are better matched with phase tuning than with position tuning. This result identifies a practical difference between two biologically motivated implementations within this hardware system, rather than establishing a universal preference for phase encoding.
neurips-2003-a-neuromorphic-multi-chip-m.tldr: A two-chip spiking-neuron system implements disparity-selective vision and performs better with phase-based than position-based tuning.

paragraphs: The supplied abstract introduces interdependent security as a problem in which people make separate protective investments, but their eventual safety depends on what others do. The relevant decisions can concern physical, financial, medical, or other forms of security. The key issue is that an individual’s protection cannot always be evaluated independently of the surrounding population.

A condominium sprinkler system illustrates the reasoning. Installing sprinklers may greatly reduce damage from a fire that starts inside the owner’s unit. The same installation may provide little protection against a fire that has already grown elsewhere in the building, because sprinklers can usually extinguish only small fires at an early stage.

This dependence changes the incentive to invest. If sufficiently many neighbors leave their units unprotected, outside fire risk may make an individual installation no longer cost-effective. The example explains why a protective measure can be useful against a local hazard yet unattractive as an individual purchase. It motivates studying security investment as an interacting set of decisions across a population.
neurips-2003-algorithms-for-interdepende.tldr: Interdependent security models explain how other people’s choices can make an individually protective investment no longer cost-effective.

paragraphs: The paper examines the theoretical behavior of classification methods that choose among several categories by minimizing a risk function. These methods extend ideas from binary large-margin classification, including the use of a loss function to guide learning. The central question concerns their behavior in the infinite-sample setting, where the analysis asks what happens with unlimited data.

The authors establish conditions sufficient to guarantee consistency within this framework. This gives a way to distinguish formulations whose limiting classification behavior is justified by the theory. They illustrate the general formulation with two specific forms that extend several existing methods. The guarantee depends on the stated conditions; it is not a blanket guarantee for every multicategory risk-minimization method.

The examples also show that some formulations can recover conditional class probabilities. Such estimates describe how likely each category is for a given observation, providing information beyond a single predicted label. The contribution therefore connects multicategory classification theory with probability estimation, which the authors identify as useful for statistical inference tasks extending beyond classification itself.
neurips-2003-an-infinity-sample-theory-f.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for infinite-sample consistency of multicategory risk minimization and shows that some formulations also estimate class probabilities.

paragraphs: This paper develops an analytical approximation to bootstrap averages for support vector classification. The object of interest is an average over bootstrap samples, so the calculation concerns behavior across resampled datasets rather than only one fitted classifier. The authors seek to approximate that average through a mathematical calculation.

Their method combines two technical approaches: the replica method from statistical physics and the TAP approach to approximate inference. These are brought together to compute the bootstrap averages. The distinction between an analytical approximation and a directly sampled average is central: the proposed method provides another route to the same averaging problem, with approximation built into its formulation.

The authors test the method on a few datasets and compare its outputs with reference averages obtained through extensive Monte Carlo sampling. That comparison provides a way to assess the analytical approximation against a sampling-based calculation. The stated contribution is the computation method and this empirical comparison; the abstract does not report a particular accuracy advantage or computational speedup.
neurips-2003-approximate-analytical-boot.tldr: The paper combines replica and TAP methods to approximate bootstrap averages for support vector classifiers and compares them with Monte Carlo averages.

paragraphs: Bootstrap sampling is often used to explore uncertainty about a model’s structure. This paper shows through experiments on artificial and real-world data that graphical models learned from bootstrap samples can be strongly biased toward excessive complexity. Consequently, variation among the learned graphs can reflect a systematic distortion introduced by resampling.

The authors connect this distortion to spurious dependencies induced by the bootstrap. Such dependencies can make additional structure appear warranted. They derive a leading-order correction equal to half of Akaike’s model-complexity penalty and demonstrate its effect experimentally. The correction targets the tendency to favor overly elaborate graphs when using bootstrap results to assess structural uncertainty.

The analysis also relates the effect to bias in the plug-in entropy estimator and to the difference between expected training and test errors. These connections distinguish two penalty sizes: the bootstrap correction is half of Akaike’s penalty, while the expected test–training error difference approaches the full penalty asymptotically. Keeping these quantities separate matters when interpreting or correcting the respective biases.
neurips-2003-bias-corrected-bootstrap-an.tldr: Bootstrap samples can favor overly complex graphical models, and the paper derives a leading-order correction equal to half of Akaike’s complexity penalty.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification of deformable, three-dimensional free-form shapes represented by range data. Its task is to recognize shape categories, even when members of a category vary in form. This differs from matching a particular object through alignment, which the abstract identifies as the focus of traditional systems using surface signatures.

The proposed method adapts a symbolic-signature representation to describe shape classes. An ensemble of classifiers learns parts associated with each class and the geometric relationships among those parts. It uses both numerical and symbolic descriptors, building an abstract class description from information about components and how they fit together.

The authors evaluate the classification system in large-scale discrimination experiments involving two well-defined classes that share many distinctive features. Their results suggest better performance than traditional numerical signature methods. This is evidence for the approach in the studied comparison, with the shared features making the distinction between the two classes especially relevant. The contribution is a class-oriented representation of deformable shape through learned parts and relationships.
neurips-2003-discriminating-deformable-s.tldr: An ensemble learns shape parts and their geometric relationships, with experiments suggesting improved discrimination of two deformable 3-D shape classes.

paragraphs: Algorithms that combine expert advice commonly compare their rewards with what the best expert would have earned along the same sequence of environmental states. This comparison becomes problematic when chosen actions influence future states. In repeated games, for example, a player’s behavior can change how an opponent responds, so the future depends on the strategy actually followed.

The paper presents and analyzes an expert-combination algorithm that considers these longer-term effects. Under certain conditions, its performance asymptotically matches that of the best available expert. The qualification matters: the result concerns long-run behavior under the analysis’s conditions, rather than an unconditional guarantee at every stage of interaction.

The repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma demonstrates why this change in perspective can matter. The proposed algorithm can induce cooperation, whereas the previous expert algorithms discussed in the abstract converge to inferior noncooperative play. This example connects the theoretical motivation to behavior: evaluating advice must sometimes account for how following it reshapes the opponent’s future actions, as well as the rewards obtained immediately.
neurips-2003-how-to-combine-expert-and-n.tldr: An expert-combination algorithm accounts for actions’ effects on future interaction and, under conditions, asymptotically matches the best expert.

paragraphs: Face detection illustrates a severe imbalance between targets and nontargets. An image can contain millions of candidate windows of the right size, while only a few contain faces. The paper builds on the cascade architecture used by Viola and Jones, which addresses this rare-event setting through a sequence of classification stages.

The contribution is a new way to learn the cascade using forward feature selection. Feature selection is a central component of the earlier approach, where it is based on AdaBoost. By changing this learning component, the authors target the work needed to construct the detector while retaining classifiers of equivalent quality.

The paper reports that its cascade-learning method is two orders of magnitude faster than the Viola–Jones approach. This is a claim about learning the classifier, rather than a stated speedup in running the finished detector. The authors suggest that faster learning could make more demanding uses, such as online learning, feasible. That application remains a proposed possibility in the abstract.
neurips-2003-learning-a-rare-event-detec.tldr: Forward feature selection learns rare-event detection cascades two orders of magnitude faster than the Viola–Jones approach while yielding equivalent classifier quality.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a neural architecture that learns relationships between perceptions and actions and uses those relationships to plan behavior. Its world model consists of learned states and knowledge of possible transitions between them. The same architecture therefore supports both representing experience and organizing actions through the learned representation.

A growing, self-organizing layer learns the state representations and connects directly to perception and motor layers. Connections within the state layer encode which transitions are possible. Motor signals modulate these connections, linking the transition model to action. A dynamic field on the layer then organizes the planning process through activity in this connected state representation.

All the proposed mechanisms are local, and adaptation follows Hebbian ideas about learning through related activity. The model also operates continuously in perception, action, and time. Together, these properties describe how the authors integrate learning and planning within a dynamic neural system. The contribution is the architecture and its coordinated mechanisms for turning learned perception–action relationships into behavioral planning.
neurips-2003-learning-a-world-model-and-.tldr: A self-organizing neural architecture learns perception–action transitions and uses locally interacting dynamics to plan behavior.

paragraphs: K-means requires a choice of how many clusters to find, but that number is often unclear before examining the data. G-means addresses this choice during clustering. It uses a statistical test of whether the data assigned to a cluster follow a Gaussian distribution, making distributional evidence central to deciding the number of clusters.

The algorithm runs k-means hierarchically with increasing numbers of clusters. It stops when the test accepts the Gaussian hypothesis for the data associated with every center. Its single user parameter is the statistical significance level. The authors emphasize that the test neither restricts covariance nor requires computing a full covariance matrix.

Experiments show favorable results compared with a recent method using the Bayesian information criterion to penalize model complexity. In those experiments, the BIC penalty was too weak to provide an effective score. The finding supports G-means in the tested settings, while its stopping rule remains tied to testing Gaussian structure within clusters. Acceptance by the test supplies the algorithm’s decision criterion, rather than proof of Gaussianity.
neurips-2003-learning-the-k-in-k-means-5.tldr: G-means chooses the number of clusters by increasing k until statistical tests accept Gaussian structure within each cluster.

paragraphs: The paper studies the eigenvalue spectrum of sample covariance matrices when variation is stronger in some directions than others. For ordinary PCA, it considers a small number of directions with increased variance. The analysis asks how these underlying signals appear in the spectrum calculated from sampled data, and how sampling affects their apparent strength.

The results use a high-dimensional limit with the ratio of sample size to dimension held fixed. The spectrum depends on this ratio and on signal strength. As the ratio increases, transitions occur in which distinct spectral masses emerge above the main bulk, corresponding to the special directions. The authors also calculate bias in the associated eigenvalues.

For kernel PCA, the relevant covariance exists in feature space. The authors show that this space can contain directional structure even when the original data components are independent and have equal variance. Their examples exhibit transitions analogous to those for ordinary PCA. These results connect sampling, dimensionality, and feature-space structure to when distinguished components become visible in the spectrum.
neurips-2003-limiting-form-of-the-sample.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis characterizes when signal-related eigenvalues separate from the covariance spectrum’s bulk in PCA and analogous kernel PCA examples.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a model to order every label in a predefined set for each input. This paper develops a supervised batch-learning framework for that task. Training examples provide preferences among labels, but those preferences may omit comparisons or even contradict one another. The desired prediction is nevertheless a complete ordering of all labels.

This separation between flexible supervision and a fully ordered output lets the framework accommodate different kinds of ranking problems. The authors identify multilabel categorization and hierarchical classification as special cases. The approach therefore connects several prediction settings through the common problem of learning an overall label order from the preferences available in training.

The paper introduces a general boosting-based learning algorithm and proves a lower bound on the progress made in each boosting iteration. That result supplies theoretical information about the learning procedure’s advancement. Experiments on a large-scale text corpus demonstrate the approach’s applicability. Together, the contributions address both learning from imperfect preference information and producing complete rankings from it.
neurips-2003-log-linear-models-for-label.tldr: A boosting-based framework learns complete label rankings from preference lists that may be incomplete or inconsistent.

paragraphs: The User Rating Profile model describes collaborative filtering through a generative account of users’ ratings. Its underlying process is designed to produce a complete profile: one rating for every item for each user. This provides a model of how a user’s set of ratings could arise from hidden preferences.

Each user is represented as a mixture of attitudes, with the mixture proportions governed by a Dirichlet random variable. To generate an item’s rating, the model first chooses an attitude for that item. It then draws a rating according to the preference pattern associated with the chosen attitude. Different items can consequently draw on different attitudes within the same user’s mixture.

The key representational idea is to describe a person through several attitudes and their proportions, while retaining an item-by-item rating process. The authors relate URP to multinomial mixtures, the aspect model, and latent Dirichlet allocation, and claim advantages over each. The concrete mechanism supplied here is the combination of user-level mixtures with attitude-based generation of individual ratings.
neurips-2003-modeling-user-rating-profil.tldr: The User Rating Profile model generates ratings by representing each user as a mixture of attitudes and selecting an attitude for each item.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a nonlinear form of Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) for observations that share underlying low-dimensional coordinates but appear on different high-dimensional manifolds. The aim is to connect these different representations through their shared coordinates. This extends nonlinear dimensionality reduction to a setting with multiple representations of the same underlying structure.

The method coordinates, or aligns, mixtures of linear models. Its central idea is to build a nonlinear approach by bringing these linear models into agreement. The paper also establishes a connection to an existing dimensionality-reduction method: a special case, applied to a single manifold, reduces to Laplacian Eigenmaps. This ties the proposed approach to both multiple-representation analysis and single-manifold dimensionality reduction.

After the mixture models have been estimated, all parameters of the proposed model can be calculated in closed form, without local optima in that learning stage. That qualification matters: the claim concerns estimation after the mixtures are available. The experimental results illustrate that the approach is viable as a nonlinear extension of CCA, supporting its use for the shared-coordinate setting described by the authors.
neurips-2003-non-linear-cca-and-pca-by-a.tldr: The paper extends CCA to nonlinear representations by aligning mixtures of linear models, with a single-manifold special case that recovers Laplacian Eigenmaps.

paragraphs: The paper challenges a purely linear account of how neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus respond to visual input. Motivated by evidence of nonlinear responses, the authors propose a model combining a linear receptive field with a nonlinear suppressive field. The model brings together findings from more than three decades of research.

The suppressive field measures local root-mean-square contrast and acts divisively on the response. In plain language, the model combines filtering of the visual pattern with a contrast-dependent adjustment of response strength. This gives a specific mechanism for nonlinear behavior while retaining a linear component in the description of what stimulates the neuron.

The authors test the model using recordings from the LGN of anesthetized, paralyzed cats. Parameters estimated from a basic measurement set allow accurate predictions for novel stimuli. These results support the joint use of linear filtering and divisive gain control in the studied responses. The authors propose that the model might become a new standard account of LGN processing, presenting that status as a possibility.
neurips-2003-nonlinear-processing-in-lgn.tldr: A model combining linear filtering with contrast-dependent divisive suppression accurately predicts novel-stimulus responses in recorded cat LGN neurons.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression uses a covariance function to express relationships between function values. This paper introduces covariance functions that can vary with location in the input space. Such nonstationary models can adapt when the function being learned is smoother in some regions than in others.

The proposed class includes a nonstationary form of the Matérn covariance. A parameter controls differentiability, allowing that property to be represented within the model rather than fixed in advance. This combines adaptation across inputs with control over how smoothly the regression function behaves. The authors also state that the model readily extends to non-Gaussian data.

Experiments show strong performance in two and three input dimensions: the model outperforms a neural network and Bayesian free-knot spline models while remaining competitive with a Bayesian neural network. In one dimension, a state-of-the-art Bayesian free-knot spline model performs better. The authors suggest that methods for accelerating GP fitting may enable larger datasets, so that scalability extension is presented as a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.
neurips-2003-nonstationary-covariance-fu.tldr: Nonstationary Gaussian process covariances adapt to changing smoothness and show favorable, dimension-dependent regression results.

paragraphs: Salinity sensors in the Columbia River Estuary monitoring system can gradually become fouled by biological growth. This degradation corrupts measurements needed to understand the estuary. Detecting its onset is difficult because examples are scarce and the pattern of degradation varies, making conventional discrimination between healthy and fouled sensors challenging.

The authors use novelty detection together with a parameterized model of bio-fouling. This incorporates an explicit description of the fault into the detection approach. The detectors identify both whether fouling has occurred and when it began, with reliability comparable to human experts. Early identification matters because it can reduce the amount of corrupted sensor data.

During the reported initial real-time deployment, the detectors produced no false alarms and caught every degradation episode before field staff scheduled the sensors for cleaning. Across the longer period reported in the abstract, they essentially doubled the useful data obtained from the sensors. These are deployment findings for the monitoring system studied, linking fault detection to a substantial practical improvement in data availability.
neurips-2003-parameterized-novelty-detec.tldr: Novelty detectors incorporating a bio-fouling model identified sensor degradation early and essentially doubled useful data in the reported estuary deployment.

paragraphs: The paper studies policy search in reinforcement learning, where learning focuses on finding a rule for choosing actions. Its central starting point is a supplied baseline distribution over states. This distribution indicates, approximately, how often a good policy is expected to visit each state, giving the algorithm information about which states matter for successful behavior.

Given that distribution, the authors derive a policy-search algorithm that terminates after finitely many steps and has nontrivial performance guarantees. These are distinct contributions: finite termination concerns completion of the procedure, while the guarantees concern the quality of its resulting behavior. Both are presented within a framework that assumes the baseline distribution is available.

The algorithm is demonstrated on several grid-world problems with partial observability, a planar biped walking robot, and double-pole balancing. These examples cover different action-selection settings in which the proposed approach can be applied. The paper’s stated significance is the connection between approximate knowledge of good-policy state visitation and a policy-search procedure with finite termination and meaningful theoretical performance guarantees.
neurips-2003-policy-search-by-dynamic-pr.tldr: Given a baseline distribution describing good-policy state visitation, the paper derives a finitely terminating policy-search algorithm with performance guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper proposes ranking data according to the underlying geometric structure revealed by a collection of examples. It addresses data represented in Euclidean space, including text and images. The central idea is that a large dataset can reveal an intrinsic manifold, and that this collective structure should inform how its elements are ranked.

The motivation comes from web ranking that exploits global hyperlink structure through random walks. For the proposed setting, the relevant structure comes from the data’s geometry. This shifts attention toward relationships visible across the collection: the ranking is intended to reflect the manifold on which the data lie, rather than relying only on local relationships.

The authors report encouraging experiments using synthetic data, images, and text. Those results illustrate the validity of the method across the tested kinds of data. The contribution is a simple, broadly intended ranking approach organized around intrinsic data structure. Its practical appeal is the possibility of using the geometry collectively revealed by many examples to guide rankings across different data types.
neurips-2003-ranking-on-data-manifolds-b.tldr: The paper ranks Euclidean-space data using the intrinsic manifold structure revealed collectively by the dataset.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how neural networks can represent logical reasoning about time and knowledge. Temporal logic expresses relationships involving time, while modal logics of knowledge represent what agents know. The authors show that temporal logic and combinations of these two kinds of logic can be represented effectively within artificial neural networks.

Their main construction is an algorithm that translates temporal rules into networks. They show that the resulting networks compute a fixed-point semantics for those rules: the network computation corresponds to a stable interpretation of the logical system. This provides a formal connection between the rules being represented and the computation performed by the neural implementation.

The translation is applied to the muddy children puzzle, a test problem for distributed multi-agent systems. Simple neural networks provide a complete solution while supporting temporal reasoning and knowledge acquisition through inductive learning. The contribution combines a translation procedure, a semantics result, and an application showing how logical reasoning and learning can coexist in the proposed neural systems.
neurips-2003-reasoning-about-time-and-kn.tldr: A translation from temporal rules to neural networks preserves fixed-point semantics and supports a complete solution to the muddy children puzzle.

paragraphs: A Markov decision problem requires probabilities describing how actions move the system between states. The paper addresses the sensitivity of optimal solutions to errors in those probabilities. Since transition estimates can be inaccurate in practical applications, a policy optimized for the estimated model may depend heavily on uncertain information.

The authors propose an algorithm for problems with finite state and action sets that explicitly represents transition uncertainty. They use bounds based on Kullback–Leibler divergence, describing the representation as statistically accurate and numerically efficient. The resulting solution has a robustness guarantee with respect to transition-estimation errors covered by this uncertainty representation.

The algorithm’s worst-case complexity matches that of the original Bellman recursion. The authors consequently argue that robustness can be introduced at practically no extra computational cost. This combines two aims that matter together: accounting for uncertain dynamics and preserving computational tractability. The guarantee concerns the modeled transition uncertainty in the stated finite setting, while the complexity result explains why incorporating that uncertainty need not change the worst-case computational order.
neurips-2003-robustness-in-markov-decisi.tldr: An algorithm uses KL-divergence bounds to make finite MDP solutions robust to transition uncertainty while matching Bellman recursion’s worst-case complexity.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for approximating marginal probabilities in graphical models containing cycles. It combines a Gaussian entropy bound with a semidefinite outer bound on the marginal polytope, the set describing feasible marginals. Together, these ingredients produce a log-determinant optimization problem that can be solved with efficient interior-point methods.

The optimizing arguments are used as approximations to the true marginals. The variational formulation is strictly convex and therefore has a unique global optimum, distinguishing its optimization behavior from Bethe and Kikuchi approaches. Its optimal value also provides a guaranteed upper bound on the log partition function. That guarantee concerns the normalization-related quantity, rather than making the approximate marginals exact.

In experiments, the relaxation performs comparably to or better than sum-product, with substantial improvements for certain problem classes. The authors also show that its zero-temperature limit recovers known semidefinite relaxations for integer programming. The contribution thus links approximate probabilistic inference to a well-behaved optimization problem with a bound guarantee and a connection to discrete optimization.
neurips-2003-semidefinite-relaxations-fo.tldr: A log-determinant relaxation approximates marginals on cyclic graphs with a unique global optimum and a guaranteed upper bound on the log partition function.

paragraphs: This paper asks why sensory inputs are separated into modalities in the way they are. It examines that question through self-supervised learning between vision and hearing. The authors use the Minimizing-Disagreement algorithm for unsupervised speech categorization, with moving lips providing visual information and the sound signal providing auditory information.

The striking experiment changes which side of the network receives certain auditory dimensions. Although those dimensions are highly informative, moving them to the visual side harms performance. In the studied setting, discarding them works better than treating them as part of the visual input. Their usefulness therefore depends on how they are grouped with the other sensory information.

The authors explain this result through the statistical structure of sensory inputs and argue that the usual modality separation is well suited to cross-modal learning. The finding shows why informative features alone do not determine success: the relationships within and between the input groups also matter. Its evidence comes from the reported speech-categorization task and the specific reassignment of auditory information.
neurips-2003-sensory-modality-segregatio.tldr: In cross-modal speech learning, moving informative auditory features to the visual input harms performance more than discarding them.

paragraphs: The paper presents an unsupervised algorithm for learning linguistic structure from a plain natural-language corpus. It addresses both the acquisition of structured knowledge from substantial text collections and generalization to unseen text. The aim is a compact representation built from patterns discovered in the language data.

Sentences are represented as paths through a graph whose vertices initially correspond to words or word parts. Recursive statistical inference uses context to identify significant patterns, which become new vertices. Linguistic constructions are then represented as trees composed of these patterns and their associated equivalence classes. This allows discovered structure to become part of the representation used for further learning.

An input module lets the system take a standard English-as-a-Second-Language proficiency test. Its performance reaches a level described as intermediate for ninth-grade students, despite training on CHILDES transcripts of parents speaking to young children. This is an encouraging test result for generalization from that corpus. It describes performance on the proficiency assessment, rather than establishing equivalence to a student’s overall language abilities.
neurips-2003-unsupervised-context-sensit.tldr: An unsupervised graph-based language learner discovers contextual patterns and achieves an intermediate ninth-grade ESL test level after training on child-directed speech.
